title: US Proposes Tougher PERM Green Card Test: 90-Day Recruitment, Two-Year Layoff Bar
excerpt: A Labor Department proposal would end the Schedule A shortcut, triple the minimum recruitment period, and bar employers from sponsoring green cards within two years of similar-role US layoffs. It is a proposal only — comments run 60 days from November 17.
body:
• The US Department of Labor has proposed rewriting the PERM labor certification — the labour-market test most employer-sponsored green cards must pass — with a uniform electronic recruitment process, an end to the Schedule A shortcut for nurses, physical therapists and exceptional-ability workers, and far stricter layoff rules.
  • Employers would have to advertise for at least 90 days (up from a 30-day state job order today) and attest they have not laid off US workers in the same or similar occupation at the same workplace in the two years before filing — up from a six-month consideration duty.
  • Nothing changes yet: this is a proposed rule, scheduled for Federal Register publication on November 17, 2026, with public comments open for 60 days after publication. Nearly 60% of PERM applications are filed for workers currently in H-1B status, the Labor Department says.

The Trump administration has proposed a sweeping rewrite of the rules US employers must follow to sponsor foreign workers for green cards, tightening the labour-market test at the heart of the PERM programme and barring companies from filing at all if they have recently laid off American workers in similar roles. The Department of Labor's notice of proposed rulemaking, titled "Modernizing the Labor Market Test and Improving Protections for U.S. Workers in the PERM Immigrant Visa Program," was released for public inspection on November 16 and is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on November 17, 2026.

Who this touches — exactly

PERM is the permanent labor certification an employer must usually obtain before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based green card in the EB-2 and EB-3 categories: the employer must show that qualified US workers are unavailable and that the hire will not adversely affect the pay or working conditions of similarly employed Americans. Counted here: employer-sponsored EB-2 and EB-3 cases that require labor certification. Not counted: EB-2 cases where the job-offer requirement is waived in the national interest, and family-based green cards, which never pass through PERM. The exposure is large among Indian professionals in the US technology workforce: the Labor Department's proposal notes that nearly 60% of PERM applications are filed on behalf of individuals currently in H-1B status, and approximately 73% for workers on temporary nonimmigrant visas, citing its own performance data for fiscal 2021-2025. Reuters notes the programme is used heavily by large American technology companies and outsourcing firms, and Bloomberg describes it as one Silicon Valley has long used to retain overseas talent.

"workers using the latest technologies and methods," in the proposal's words."

The biggest change: a two-year layoff bar

Under the current rule, an employer that laid off workers in the area of intended employment within six months of filing must document that it notified and considered potentially qualified laid-off US workers. The proposal replaces that with a pre-filing bar: the employer must attest that it has not laid off any US workers in the same or similar occupation at the place of employment within two years before filing — and if it cannot make that attestation, it would be prohibited from filing the application. The duty would also extend after filing: employers would have to keep considering laid-off US workers through approval of the Form I-140 immigrant petition, offer the job unless there is a lawful, job-related reason for rejection, and notify the Labor Department no later than five business days after a covered post-filing layoff.

Recruitment: longer, electronic, and reported up front

The proposal replaces the current print-heavy recruitment menu — a 30-day state workforce agency job order, Sunday newspaper advertising and additional steps for professional occupations — with a uniform electronic set built around employer websites, job-search websites, social media platforms and job fairs or campus recruiting. Advertising, including the state job order, would have to run for no less than 90 calendar days, or the employer's customary advertising period for the occupation over the previous 12 months, whichever is longer. Recruitment would have to be completed no more than 60 and no fewer than 30 calendar days before filing, and employers would submit a recruitment report with the application itself — documenting the advertising, who applied, and why US applicants were not hired — rather than holding records against a possible audit. The Labor Department says the redesign is meant to "access the broadest pool of high-quality U.S. workers using the latest technologies and methods," in the proposal's words. Mandatory newspaper advertising would be eliminated.

Schedule A shortcut would end

The proposal would end the department's administration of Schedule A — described in the rule as "eliminating further administration of Schedule A, which exempts certain job opportunities from the statutorily required labor market test." Schedule A currently lets employers skip the labour-market test entirely for physical therapists and professional nurses, and for people of exceptional ability in the sciences, arts or performing arts, filing directly with USCIS alongside Form I-140. The Labor Department argues it lacks authority to exempt occupations from the statutory test and can no longer demonstrate a nationwide shortage for the listed occupations with a reliable methodology. A single set of recruitment requirements would apply to all occupations — a change analysts note would particularly affect hospitals sponsoring nurses and physical therapists. The proposal also enhances debarment — extending it across all Labor Department labour certification and labour condition programmes — and codifies mandatory electronic filing.

What to do next

For workers with a PERM case in preparation or pending, the immediate answer is that nothing has changed: this is a proposal, not a final rule, and it does not alter any employer's obligations today. The comment period runs for 60 days after the November 17 publication; comments can be filed through regulations.gov under Docket No. ETA-2026-0133, and the department must consider them before issuing any final rule. If a final rule is published, the proposal sketches a 90-day transition — a 60-day delayed effective date plus a further 30 days — before the new requirements bite, though analysts caution those arrangements could change before finalisation. A separate October action, in which Reuters reported the government blocked major technology companies including Microsoft, the largest PERM filer per Labor Department data, from using the programme, is not part of this rulemaking. Workers whose employers are planning layoffs, or whose sponsorship depends on Schedule A, have the most reason to raise the proposal with their employer's immigration counsel now rather than after a final rule appears.
